🥸 Crypto phishing: how to stay safe

Scammers impersonate trusted sources to steal your data or money. In crypto, it's especially dangerous — transactions can't be reversed.

Three most common scams.

1⃣ Fake website
You search for Wallet on Google, click the first link, and land on a clone. The address looks almost real, but something's off: wa1let tg, wall3t-tg, etc. You enter your details and they go straight to scammers. 

How to check: @wallet works inside Telegram. There's no separate login website.

2⃣ Fake bot
A bot called "Wallet Support" messages you asking to verify your account or share a code. It looks convincing: icon, description, even reviews.

How to check: there's only one official support bot @wallet_supportbot. No others exist.

3⃣ Message from "the team"
"Your account is blocked", "Verify your identity immediately", "You've won a prize." The goal is always the same: get you to click a link or hand over your details.

How to check: Wallet Support never messages first and never asks for codes. All official communications come through verified social channels or the mini app.

💡 The golden rule: verify the source before entering anything. And keep our official channels handy so you always know where the real Wallet is.

📌 Rollup Sequencers: The Gatekeepers of Layer 2 Blocks

Main Points
⏺ Sequencers order transactions on Layer 2 and send batches to the base chain
⏺ They control UX: speed, ordering, and sometimes fees
⏺ This post explains why sequencers are crucial for rollups — and why decentralizing them matters

1️⃣ Role — sequencers receive user transactions, decide their order, and produce L2 blocks or batches.
2️⃣ Fast UX — they can give near-instant confirmations on L2 while final settlement still happens on L1.
3️⃣ Centralization Risk — many rollups start with a single sequencer, which can censor or reorder transactions.
4️⃣ MEV & Fairness — who controls ordering also touches MEV, so sequencer design affects how value is captured or shared.
5️⃣ Roadmap — serious rollups work toward decentralized or shared-sequencer models to reduce trust assumptions.

Final Thoughts

Sequencers are the “traffic controllers” of rollups — invisible to most users, but central to how fair, fast, and decentralized Layer 2 really is.

Something I realize more and more, with trading but also with life, is that not everything is under our control, and that more is not necessarily better.

For example, I've been bullish since January/February, when price reached the expected main support zone of $60k-70k:

[https://t.me/CryptoCapoTG_Official/1004], [https://x.com/CryptoCapo_/status/2019434869001195948?s=20]

Since then, 5 months have passed by, which is a lot of time. And price went up to 82k, then back down to 58k, and now trading at around 63k.

During all this time, of course I've reviewed my analysis to see if something was wrong and if price could go lower from here. But, the more I checked, the more it confirmed the bullish bias.

So... to what extent is it healthy to keep checking, to try to control every variable?

In the end, the result is not up to us. Market analysis doesn't give you 100% probabilities, never. There are no guarantees. You can position yourself on the side of probability, and that's what matters. But even more important is knowing how to wait, to have patience. 

And overanalyzing, besides causing unnecessary stress, can make you change your mind simply because what you expect is not happening yet.

The market could remain within a range for more weeks, or it could start going up from here. That's difficult to know. What you need to know is how to not let that affect you while you keep living your life, and how to adapt if something unexpected occurs.

Therefore, the lesson here is trust, acceptance, and detachment. Trust because you've done your best. Acceptance to embrace the reality of the present moment and its timing. And detachment by understanding that the final outcome doesn't fully depend on you. That depends on something much bigger than us.

And this applies to everything in life.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

"Introduction to Machine Learning" is another free textbook on machine learning, approximately 600 pages long, which emphasizes a deep mathematical understanding of the subject. 📚🧮

The book begins with the mathematical foundations necessary for further study: linear algebra, mathematical analysis, probability theory, matrix analysis, and optimization methods. It then covers the main supervised learning algorithms: linear and logistic regression, the k-nearest neighbors method, decision trees, random forests, boosting, and neural networks. 🤖📈

A significant portion of the book is dedicated to probabilistic and generative models. It discusses Monte Carlo methods, graphical models, Bayesian networks, variational methods, normalizing flows, variational autoencoders (VAEs), and generative adversarial networks (GANs). 🎲🧠

The final chapters discuss clustering, principal component analysis (PCA), learning on manifolds, and theoretical estimates of a model's ability to generalize. 🔍📊

In my opinion, this is an excellent resource for those who want to gain a broad understanding of machine learning and understand the mathematics underlying the key methods, rather than treating them as "black boxes." 💡✨

Indian Government vs Students: Who Will Hang Tough? 


When thousands of unarmed students marched toward the Indian Parliament building last month in a rare challenge to the government, they were met by a wall of riot police officers determined to stop them.

Officials had blocked internet in the area, initially slowing the emergence of details of the crackdown. But videos taken by protesters and witnesses began circulating, revealing that security forces beat people with sticks and fired tear gas and pellet guns at them. The footage led to accusations of excessive force being wielded against peaceful demonstrators.

The New York Times has verified and analyzed images and video footage shared by protesters, along with witness accounts, to examine how the Delhi Police, the Rapid Action Force and other paramilitary forces handled the crowds. Several Times reporters were also present at the scene on July 20, the day of the march.

The evidence suggests that security forces exceeded many guidelines for law enforcement in peaceful demonstrations established by the United Nations and also those from India’s home ministry, which state that force “should be used when it is absolutely necessary, it should be minimum and proportional to the situation.”

While police brutality is not unusual in India, especially against minority groups, there was public outrage over how the authorities repressed a vast crowd of young people demanding accountability for the nation’s flawed education system. Protest organizers said at least 150 participants were hospitalized and many more injured. Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in the lower house of Parliament, has condemned the use of “brute” force, saying, “the assault on students is a stain on our democratic country.”

The Delhi Police has said that no permission had been sought or granted for the march, which demonstrators called for after several weeks of peaceful protest at a site near Parliament. 

The police said the march was “strictly prohibited” and that force had been used as a last resort. They said that 118 police personnel had been injured and that 70 people had been detained for violations of law and order. 

The Delhi Police did not respond to requests for comment on the video findings documented by The Times.

Security forces used lathis — long batons made out of bamboo or polycarbonate — to hit protesters, a tactic commonly used to control crowds if they become unruly and don’t respond to whistles or warnings delivered over loudspeakers. Security forces are advised to avoid overarm strikes and to hit people on their arms or legs, according to U.N. guidelines. But multiple accounts and videos verified by The Times appear to show police personnel, and a man in plainclothes, aiming for protesters’ torsos.

Tear gas, which irritates the eyes, throat and lungs, was widely used to break up large crowds gathered in the areas adjacent to the designated protest site. 

U.N. guidelines say tear gas should never be used to disperse peaceful protesters. Typically, the canisters should be fired in an arc and not directly toward a crowd, but videos verified by The Times showed security forces releasing tear gas by hand at a lower trajectory.

Many protesters who were detained or targeted by security forces in Delhi or elsewhere have filed petitions with the Supreme Court, accusing the security forces of brutality and seeking punishment for those involved. 

The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party — a once satirical group that led the youth movement — have urged protesters to preserve videos and photos as evidence, saying that dozens of people detained could face charges despite government assurances that they would not be.

While hearing petitions filed by protesters on July 28, the Supreme Court of India said that there should be an “evidence-based inquiry” into whether excessive force was used.

📣 EU to revise MiCA rules in 2027 amid US stablecoin push 

⚠️ European Union officials are preparing to revise the bloc’s MiCA crypto framework in 2027 as foreign stablecoin restrictions and faster U.S. rulemaking expose gaps in the existing regime. The planned revision would examine how MiCA treats stablecoins issued outside the European Union. Current requirements have prevented several foreign issuers from receiving authorization, limiting their access to regulated exchanges across the bloc.

💬 “Reopening the file seems unavoidable at this stage,” an unidentified European diplomat told Euronews.

🔗 The diplomat cited positions taken by European institutions, including the European Central Bank, along with changes in global regulation and digital-asset technology. No final proposal has been published. Any amendment would need to pass through the EU’s legislative process before taking effect. The consultation covers developments that have occurred since MiCA entered into application. Its deadline has been extended to Sept. 30, with crypto issuers, service providers, regulators, central banks and finance ministries invited to respond.

From 2018 to 2023, I was the lead database administrator for a black-site medical facility. My clearance was TS/SCI. My job was to ensure the local servers synced perfectly with the Pentagon's main medical grid.

The facility had four levels. Levels 1 through 3 were standard military trauma care. Level 4 was restricted. Even with my clearance, my badge wouldn't open the elevator doors to Level 4.

But I could see the data traffic coming from it.

Every time a session was initiated on Level 4, the servers would process massive amounts of genomic data. We are talking terabytes of information per second. It wasn't just reading DNA — it was rewriting it. 

⟁

I started running silent queries on the patient IDs coming out of Level 4. I cross-referenced them with the civilian medical database. 

Patient 884-A: 62-year-old male. Civilian diagnosis: Stage 4 Glioblastoma (terminal brain cancer). Admitted to Level 4 on a Tuesday. Discharged on a Friday. Civilian database updated: "Spontaneous remission."

Patient 912-C: 45-year-old female. Civilian diagnosis: Advanced Multiple Sclerosis. Wheelchair-bound. Admitted to Level 4 for two weeks. Civilian database updated: "Misdiagnosis. Patient exhibits full motor function."

They weren't spontaneous remissions. They weren't misdiagnoses. They were cures.

⟁

I tracked 314 patients over five years. Every single one went into Level 4 with a terminal or incurable condition. Every single one came out completely healed.

He looked at me, dead serious, and said, "We are. But the economy runs on treatment, son. It doesn't run on cures. Forget what you saw."

I couldn't forget. I downloaded the server logs to an encrypted drive and walked out.
